opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a lot of scope, probably more than people intuitively expect. It helps to separate a few different ways AIs could end up more efficient than humans at AI R&D.

The first is just serial speed and cost. Once you have AIs that are roughly as good as a decent research engineer, you can run them much faster than a human thinks, and run huge numbers of copies in parallel. Even if they were only human-level in quality, that's already a big multiplier on the effective labor going into AI research. Labs are bottlenecked on talented people, and suddenly you'd have the equivalent of tens or hundreds of thousands of them.

The second is that AIs don't have to stay at human level. Humans are the stupidest possible species that could build a technological civilization, in some sense; we're not near any fundamental ceiling on research taste or ability. So I'd expect AIs to continue past the level of the best human researchers, and the gap between a median researcher and a top researcher is already large. You could imagine AIs being much better at things like generating and prioritizing ideas, noticing what's going wrong in an experiment, or having good intuitions about what will scale.

Third, there are structural advantages. AIs can share context much more directly, they don't need to sleep, they can be copied once one has learned something useful, and you can specialize them heavily. A lot of human research inefficiency is coordination overhead and ramp-up time, and much of that could go away.

The important caveat is compute. A lot of AI progress comes from running experiments, and if you have vastly more researcher labor but the same compute, you'll hit diminishing returns. I don't think that's a hard wall, though. Better researchers can use compute much more efficiently: run smaller experiments that extrapolate well, avoid wasted runs, find algorithmic improvements that effectively multiply your compute. So my guess is that once you get to AIs that can fully automate AI research, you could plausibly see progress speed up several-fold or more, at least for a while. There's real uncertainty about how long that lasts before you run into limits on algorithmic progress.

That's a big part of why I focus on this regime. It could arrive fairly suddenly, and it's exactly the point where it becomes hard for humans to oversee what's going on. If AIs are doing most of the research, including safety research, you really want to know whether you can trust them, or at least be able to control them if you can't.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a huge amount of scope, honestly. The way I'd frame it is that the relevant question isn't really "can AI match the best human researchers" — it's "what happens once you have systems that are roughly at that level, and then you can run them in parallel at very high speeds." That's where things get kind of wild.

So right now, if you look at how much compute goes into AI R&D, a huge fraction is just running experiments. But a big part of the bottleneck is actually the human labor — people deciding what experiments to run, debugging, writing code, interpreting results, having ideas. And the number of really good researchers at a frontier lab is, you know, hundreds, maybe low thousands if you're being generous about who counts.

Once you have AI systems that can do that work at roughly the level of a strong researcher, you could plausibly run — I don't know — tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands of copies, each thinking much faster than a human. Even conservatively, you're talking about something like a 10x or 30x increase in the effective research labor force, and that's before you get into the possibility that the systems are actually better than humans at this stuff.

Now, people push back and say, well, compute is the bottleneck, you can't just scale labor arbitrarily. And I think that's partially right. You can't run infinitely many experiments. But I think there's a lot you can do with more cognitive labor per unit compute — smaller-scale experiments that are more carefully designed, better extrapolation from small runs, much faster iteration on code and infrastructure, more careful thinking about what's actually worth testing. My rough guess is that you could get something like a 5x to 10x speedup in overall algorithmic progress pretty early on, even with compute fixed. And then obviously it could go further from there if the systems keep improving.

The part I'm more uncertain about is how long it takes to go from "AI is a useful assistant" to "AI is basically doing the research autonomously." There's a real question about whether there are hard-to-automate pieces — research taste, knowing which direction to push — that lag the rest. But I don't think those are fundamentally different in kind from the other stuff. I'd expect them to get automated too, maybe just a bit later. So my overall view is: very large scope, probably faster than most people's intuitions, and the main thing holding it back is just how quickly you can get to that threshold of roughly-human-level autonomous research capability.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s potentially a huge amount of scope, though it depends on what you mean by efficiency. One question is: how much research can you do for a given amount of compute? Another is: how quickly can you make progress in calendar time? AI could have a particularly large advantage on that second dimension, even if each individual AI researcher is only roughly as capable as a human researcher.

Suppose you could run thousands of copies of a very good AI researcher. They could try different ideas in parallel, run experiments, read the results, and then share what they learned. You’d still have bottlenecks — experiments take compute, and not every research problem decomposes nicely — but you could potentially compress a lot of work into a much shorter period.

Then there’s the possibility that the systems are actually better at research. Human researchers aren’t some theoretical limit on how effectively you can reason about machine learning. A system might be better at choosing experiments, noticing implications of results, or writing and debugging implementations. That could mean getting more progress out of the same experimental budget, rather than just spending more compute.

The thing I’d be cautious about is going directly from that to ‘therefore, you get an extremely fast intelligence explosion.’ You need to know how much of the process can be accelerated, how expensive the AI researchers are to run, and how much progress depends on large training runs or new hardware. But I don’t see a strong reason to expect human-level research ability to be close to the ceiling.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s potentially a huge amount of scope, though it depends on what you mean by efficiency. One question is how much useful research you can get per dollar. Another is how quickly you can make progress in calendar time. Those could look quite different.

For cost, you can imagine an AI researcher being much cheaper than a human researcher while being comparably productive. And then for speed, you could have systems thinking much faster than humans, running lots of copies, and sharing results very efficiently. So even without each system having dramatically better ideas than the best human researchers, you could get a substantial acceleration.

There are limits to that story. A lot of AI research involves running experiments, and those experiments require compute and take time. If you make the thinking part a hundred times faster, that doesn’t automatically make the whole research process a hundred times faster. You might just end up waiting for training runs.

But better researchers can also choose better experiments, get more information out of each experiment, or find ways to avoid expensive experiments altogether. So I wouldn’t treat experimental compute as a fixed bottleneck that rules out very large gains. My overall view is that there’s room for AI to substantially exceed human efficiency here, but how that translates into the speed of further AI progress is much more uncertain.
